chunks: And among what Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb narrated, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Jabbār, from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Faḍḍāl, from Ṣafwān, from Manṣūr, from Abū ʿUbaydah al-Ḥadhdhāʾ, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said:

Nosebleeding, vomiting, and using the toothpick such that it causes blood to flow—if you find something repugnant, it invalidates wudu (ablution); but if you do not find it repugnant, it does not invalidate wudu (ablution).

So these two reports bear two possible meanings: one of them is that they were issued in the context of taqiyyah, because that is the view of some of the ʿāmmah; and the second is that they are to be understood as indicating a kind of recommendation, so that the reports do not contradict one another.

key_terms.التَّخْلِيلُ: using a toothpick or cleaning between the teeth
key_terms.التَّقِيَّةِ: dissimulation for protection in a context of danger or necessity

ai.seo_question: Do nosebleeding, vomiting, or bleeding from using a toothpick invalidate wudu (ablution) in Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This report concerns whether nosebleeding, vomiting, or blood caused by using a toothpick invalidates wudu (ablution). The concluding note explains that such reports may either have been issued under taqiyyah or be understood as recommending renewal of wudu (ablution), in order to reconcile the narrations.
